```{r}
#| label: setup

# packages
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(modelsummary)

# data
df_raw <- read.csv("../data/journals.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: data

df <- df_raw |>
  mutate(subfield = as.factor(subfield),
         english = as.factor(english),
         age = 2026 - since) |>
  select(-since)
```

```{r}
#| label: models

lm1 <- lm(h5_index ~ issues, data = df)
lm2 <- lm(h5_index ~ issues + english, data = df)
lm3 <- lm(h5_index ~ issues + english + subfield, data = df)
lm4 <- lm(h5_index ~ issues + english + subfield + age, data = df)
```

<!-- header 1 -->

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

<!-- paragraph 1 -->

Why do some academic journals rank higher than others on Google Scholar? This paper introduces a new dataset on the rankings of fictitious journals, and uses it to explore what predicts their impact.\
Journals that publish more issues, and those that publish in English, have higher scores. Specialised journals, by contrast, have lower scores than generalist ones.

<!-- block quote -->

> All models are wrong, but some are useful.
>
> --- George E. P. Box

<!-- header 2 -->

# Introduction

<!-- paragraph 2 -->

Researchers often choose where to submit their work based on **journal rankings**. Google Scholar offers one of the most widely used rankings, based on how often the articles in each journal are cited. Yet we know little about *why some journals rank higher than others*.

<!-- paragraph 3 -->

This paper addresses this gap with a new dataset.[^data] The dataset covers journals from all continents and all major branches of science, and it is freely available.^[The data and code are available on GitHub.]

<!-- footnote 1 -->

[^data]: The dataset is fabricated for the purposes of a workshop on reproducible research. Any resemblance to real journals is coincidental.

<!-- paragraph 4 -->

The [Literature Review](#literature-review) summarises what we know about journal rankings. The following sections then introduce the hypotheses, the data, and the results.

<!-- paragraph 5 -->

The models in this paper explain a moderate share of the variation in rankings, as measured by R^2^. The findings also speak to debates on the costs of academic publishing, including the CO~2~ emissions of conference travel.

<!-- paragraph 6 -->

Journals in the dataset publish 1--12 issues per year, which makes for considerable variation. The results suggest that this variation matters --- perhaps more than is commonly assumed.

<!-- header 3 -->

# Literature Review

<!-- paragraph 7 -->

Earlier studies have linked the impact of journals to their visibility [@bennett2015]. Visibility, in turn, depends on how often and in which language journals publish [@gilbert2019, p. 126].

<!-- paragraph 8 -->

@gilbert2019 argues that frequent publication keeps journals in the minds of readers. Others focus on the role of editorial boards [for example, see @bennett2015].

<!-- paragraph 9 -->

@hirsch2005 introduced the h-index, on which the H5 Index is based. Such indices are increasingly common in studies of academic publishing [@bennett2015; @delgado2010].

<!-- paragraph 10 -->

The literature suggests two broad explanations for the success of journals, each with two components:

<!-- list -->

-   Exposure
    -   the number of issues published each year
-   Accessibility
    -   the language of publication

<!-- paragraph 11 -->

The existing publications differ in their research designs, as summarised in <!-- cross reference --> Table 1.

<!-- table 1 -->

| Author          | Year | Design       | Journal           |
|-----------------|------|--------------|-------------------|
| Bennett         | 2015 | Experimental | Journal of Bone   |
| Delgado & Perry | 2010 | Descriptive  | Journal of Route  |
| Gilbert         | 2019 | Predictive   | Journal of Ground |

<!-- paragraph 12 -->

None of these studies, however, has examined a large set of journals across disciplines. This is the contribution of the present paper.

<!-- header 4 -->

# Theory and Hypotheses

<!-- paragraph 13 -->

Journals compete for the attention of readers. Those that reach more readers are likely to be cited more, and to rank higher as a result.

<!-- header 5 -->

## First Hypothesis

<!-- paragraph 14 -->

Journals that publish more often offer more articles to cite. They also appear more often in the alerts and tables of contents that readers follow.

<!-- hypothesis 1 -->

> H1: *Journals that publish more issues per year have a higher H5 Index.*

<!-- paragraph 15 -->

This expectation should hold regardless of the discipline of journals.

<!-- header 6 -->

## Second Hypothesis

<!-- paragraph 16 -->

English is the dominant language of academic publishing. Journals that publish in English can therefore reach a larger audience.

<!-- hypothesis 2 -->

> H2: *Journals that publish in English have a higher H5 Index than those that publish in other languages.*

<!-- paragraph 17 -->

This expectation, too, should hold across disciplines.

<!-- paragraph 18 -->

Other characteristics of journals, such as their age and their focus, may matter as well. The analysis therefore controls for them.

<!-- paragraph 19 -->

The data come from Google Scholar, whose homepage is shown in <!-- cross reference --> Figure 1.

<!-- figure 1 -->

![](../image/google_scholar.png){width=60%}

<!-- paragraph 20 -->

Google Scholar ranks journals by their H5 Index and their H5 Median. Both measures are based on the articles that journals published in the last five complete years.

<!-- header 7 -->

# Data and Methods

<!-- paragraph 21 -->

There are `{r} nrow(df)` observations in the dataset. Journals come from all continents, although most are from Europe and the Americas, as <!-- cross reference --> Figure 2 shows.

<!-- figure 2 -->

```{r}
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = origin)) +
  geom_bar() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of Journals")
```

<!-- paragraph 22 -->

The analysis relies on ordinary least squares regressions, where $Y_{i}$ is the H5 Index of journal $i$ and $X_{i}$ is a set of its characteristics, as specified in <!-- cross reference --> Equation 1:

<!-- block equation -->

$$
Y_{i} = \alpha + \beta X_{i} + \varepsilon_{i}
$$

<!-- paragraph 23 -->

<!-- cross reference --> Table 2 describes the variables used in the analysis, and <!-- cross reference --> Table A1, in the Appendix, all variables in the dataset. Journals publish, on average, `{r} round(mean(df$issues), digits = 2)` issues per year.

<!-- table 2 -->

```{r}
datasummary((`H5 Index` = h5_index) + (`H5 Median` = h5_median) +
              (Issues = issues) + (Age = age) ~
              N + Mean + SD + Min + Max,
            data = df)
```

<!-- paragraph 24 -->

The H5 Index is the dependent variable. The H5 Median is closely related to it, and therefore left out of the models.

<!-- paragraph 25 -->

The number of issues is measured per year, and the age of journals in years. Language and focus are binary variables.

<!-- paragraph 26 -->

All models are estimated with the full sample of journals.

<!-- header 8 -->

# Results

<!-- paragraph 27 -->

<!-- cross reference --> Figure 3 shows a strong relationship between the two metrics of journals, in all branches of science.

<!-- figure 3 -->

```{r}
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(data = df, mapping = aes(x = h5_median, y = h5_index, color = subfield)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ branch) +
  scale_colour_discrete(name = "Journal Type", breaks = c(0, 1),
                        labels = c("Generalist", "Subfield")) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "H5 Median", y = "H5 Index")
```

<!-- paragraph 28 -->

Subfield journals tend to have lower metrics than generalist journals. This pattern is visible in every branch.

<!-- paragraph 29 -->

<!-- cross reference --> Table 3 presents the results of the regression models. According to Model 1, every additional issue that journals publish in a given year is associated with a <!-- inline code --> 1.9 increase (standard error = <!-- inline code --> 0.2) in their H5 Index.

<!-- paragraph 30 -->

The relationship remains positive and significant when the other variables are added to the model. The results thus support the first hypothesis.

<!-- table 3 -->

```{r}
modelsummary(list("Model 1" = lm1, "Model 2" = lm2,
                  "Model 3" = lm3, "Model 4" = lm4),
             coef_rename = c("issues" = "Issues", "english1" = "English",
                             "subfield1" = "Subfield", "age" = "Age",
                             "(Intercept)" = "Constant"),
             stars = c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001),
             gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"))
```

<!-- paragraph 31 -->

Journals that publish in English have a considerably higher H5 Index, in support of the second hypothesis.

<!-- paragraph 32 -->

Subfield journals have a lower H5 Index, while older journals have a slightly higher one.

<!-- header 9 -->

# Conclusion

<!-- paragraph 33 -->

This paper has introduced a new dataset on the rankings of journals. The analysis shows that exposure and accessibility both matter.

<!-- paragraph 34 -->

Future research could examine whether these patterns hold over time. It could also study the rankings of individual articles, rather than journals.

<!-- paragraph 35 -->

Finally, the paper itself is fully reproducible. Its text, data, and code are all in a single Quarto document.

<!-- header 10 -->
